Code and Lab

Research code, version records, and the planned container deployment path for a service-provider lab studying federated DDoS detection.
Published

Nov 3, 2026

The Federated DDoS Research repository holds the reusable code. Its original code and documentation use the MIT license. The repository currently provides dataset audits, bounded SGD/Adam training checks with FedAvg, portable engineering bundles, and scoped Lean proofs. These components remain research prototypes.

Open the GitHub repository

Latest Documentation Checkpoint

November 3, 2026. The nine-chapter English manuscript has been realigned with the current working study direction and four research questions with distinct roles. The checked draft has 121 PDF pages and 59 cited works. Required source data, feasibility, and the final protocol remain to be checked, and Chapter 1 awaits human review. Independent model critiques have informed the revision; they do not certify novelty or supply reviewer approval. This checkpoint adds no new training, numerical QiML engine, or final detection result. The historical software checkpoint below remains unchanged.

Current Engineering Checkpoint

November 1, 2026. The original benign-only engineering pilot completed four target cases, following 35 unit tests, the existing engineering self-test, and a synthetic integration check. The run used previously inspected development observations and preserved the publisher test boundary. It checks the software path; its outputs are not confirmatory detection results.

Grok subsequently requested revisions. Version 2 addresses confirmed issues in label and control validation, row accounting, failure reporting, Parquet engine selection, and donor seeds. The revised code passed 43 unit tests, the engineering self-test, and synthetic integration. These checks used generated fixtures. The original development run and its executed-source hash remain unchanged; version 2 has not been rerun on real data.

The revised pilot is published at commit 102293e69f2f9e7cdcac58cb12ffe8d7d0165833. Its source, regression tests, and method notes identify the reviewed version. Separate Gemini and Grok reviews both returned PASS on the supplied source and synthetic evidence. The software remains a research prototype; these reviews do not establish detection performance, independent episodes, or novelty. Exact executed-source hashes, configuration, dependency lock, and run artifacts are preserved in the private research record.

Review execution check

The two initial Grok requests were stopped by a local five-minute limit during active processing. A streamed retry also reached a fifteen-minute local limit without a final answer. The user-authorized thirty-minute retry completed in 938.566 seconds, approximately 15 minutes 39 seconds, using Grok 4.7 at high reasoning effort. Its verdict was REVISE. The local deadlines explain the earlier incomplete attempts; they are not evidence of an xAI service outage or reviewer approval.

The revised-code reviews used the same bounded packet independently. Gemini returned PASS in 156.602 seconds. Grok returned PASS in 758.709 seconds, with the reported model identifier grok-4.7-build. These are elapsed request times, not measurements of model thinking time. Neither review included a new real-data training run.

Progress records

The progress record preserves 33 of 90 recorded chapter checks and 12 of 27 Codex checks. Earlier alignment rechecks remain dated history; working-revision alignment is checked. Human checklist completion remains 0 of 15. Earlier checks remain dated workflow evidence. They do not establish chapter readiness or overall research completion. English drafting and revisions come first, followed by French translation and proofreading.

Detailed experiment and timing records remain private. No new training was performed during this literature and manuscript checkpoint, and the historical engineering checks do not establish an optimizer ranking or predict the full study runtime.

Code Versions and Results

The public project status note from November 3, 2026 records the current working-draft checkpoint and links back to this research hub. The critical literature review workflow describes how source claims, reading limits, and counterevidence are recorded.

For a reproducible result, record the full commit SHA, configuration, dependency lock, input provenance, and run identifier. A link to the current branch is useful for browsing; a commit permalink identifies the code used in a particular experiment. The repository contains citation metadata and a methodology guide.

Container Deployment

Container packaging is the proposed next distribution step. Source and build instructions will remain in GitHub, and tested images can be published in GitHub Container Registry. The registry supports public OCI images and pulls by immutable digest. No project container image has been published or tested in EVE at this stage. See the GitHub registry documentation.

A container packages an application and its dependencies. A runtime still has to start it on the destination machine. Docker separates the client that requests a pull or run from the daemon that manages images and containers. See the Docker architecture documentation.

The proposed lab route uses EVE Professional Docker nodes directly. Its cookbook documents pulling a simple third-party image with dc pull <image> on the EVE host and then selecting that image in a topology. This is documented command syntax, not a command tested with this project’s image. The dc command targets EVE’s Docker service at tcp://127.0.0.1:4243. This route does not require a separate Ubuntu guest. See section 14.6, pp. 218–219 of the EVE Professional cookbook.

The initial environment inventory recorded EVE Pro 6.5.0-27. The cited cookbook is version 7.4 and describes third-party container support dating from Pro 2.0.6-52. The feature is documented, but startup and networking with this project’s image still require checks on the installed version.

The cookbook describes running this pull from a host terminal. The website account does not itself establish host-terminal access. Acquiring the project’s own image still needs verification on the installed version. Before collecting research traffic, test the image’s startup behavior, lab interfaces, console, capture permissions, and persistence. Multi-container stacks have a separate EVE integration procedure; they should not be started beside the host’s own services without that integration.

The initial package should run the existing offline engineering checks. Packet capture, traffic generation, model inference, and a networked FL coordinator have different roles and require their own implementation and validation. Packaging the offline tools does not establish a live detector or a completed FL lab.

The website will link each published release to its code version, image digest when applicable, and supporting records. Experimental datasets, private drafts, credentials, and correspondence do not belong in the public image.
